## Jer 45 - inner-being reading

# Jeremiah 45 — inner-being scene reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per scene (provenance `jeremiah-scene-segmentation-batch7-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-baruch-seek-not · Jeremiah 45:1–5 · [D, multi] — the discouraged self-pity; seek not great things for yourself; life itself as the gift

**The reading.** A brief, tender word to Baruch, Jeremiah's faithful scribe, who has voiced his weariness: "**You said, 'Woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain; I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest'**" (v.3). God's answer both *re-frames* and *re-scales* his desire: "**Behold, what I have built I am breaking down… And do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not, for behold, I am bringing disaster upon all flesh… But I will give you your life as a prize of war in all places to which you may go**" (vv.4–5). The finding is **the *discouraged, self-pitying* servant ("woe is me… I find no rest") met with a *re-scaling of desire* — "**seek not great things for yourself**" — and the gift of *life itself*** *(stated)*. The operation is **the gentle correction of a faithful but *dispirited* interior: Baruch's real weariness and sense of unrewarded sorrow ("added sorrow to my pain… no rest") is not scolded but *re-oriented* — in a time when God is "breaking down… all flesh", the pursuit of "**great things for yourself**" (personal advancement, recognition, ease) is *out of scale* with the moment; and the promised reward is deliberately *modest and sufficient* — not greatness but *"your life"*, preserved wherever he goes** *(inferred: Baruch's complaint (v.3) is a genuine inner-being state — the *weariness and self-pity* of the faithful servant who feels his labour has brought only "sorrow upon sorrow" and "no rest"; the finding is that even the faithful can sink into *dispirited self-focus*, feeling their service unrewarded and their burden unfair; and God's response is remarkably *tender yet corrective* — not "how dare you complain" but a gentle re-framing: (1) *perspective* — "**what I have built I am breaking down… I am bringing disaster upon all flesh**" (v.4–5): the finding is that personal discouragement is re-scaled by seeing one's small sorrow *within* the vast sorrow of the age — Baruch's grief is real but it is one thread in a world-wide undoing, and this larger view *relativises* the self-pity; (2) *desire re-scaled* — "**do you seek GREAT THINGS for yourself? SEEK THEM NOT**" (v.5): the finding is that the dispirited heart's ache is partly *misdirected desire* — an expectation of "great things" (reward, status, ease) that is inappropriate to a time of judgment; the cure is to *release the pursuit of greatness* for oneself; (3) *the sufficient gift* — "**but I will give you your LIFE as a prize of war**": the finding is that God's reward to the faithful in a collapsing world is not grandeur but *preservation* — "your life", the essential and sufficient gift; the servant is taught to want *less* and to receive *enough*: not greatness, but life, kept wherever he goes)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the dispirited, self-pitying servant ("woe is me… I am weary with my groaning, and I find no rest" — even the faithful sinking into discouraged self-focus)* (thread — a gem: the weariness of the faithful who feel their service unrewarded, w/ 45:3, 1 Kgs 19:4, Ps 73:2-3, Gal 6:9); *personal sorrow re-scaled by the age's sorrow ("what I have built I am breaking down… disaster on all flesh" — one's small grief seen within the vast undoing)* (new — a gem: the larger view relativising self-pity, w/ 45:4-5); *desire re-scaled — "seek not great things for yourself" (the ache partly misdirected desire for greatness, inappropriate to the moment; the cure to release the pursuit)* (new — a gem: wanting less as the healing of discouragement, w/ 45:5, 1 Tim 6:6-8, Phil 4:11); *life itself as the sufficient gift ("I will give you your life as a prize of war" — preservation, not grandeur, as God's reward to the faithful in a collapsing world)* (new — a gem: enough, not great things, w/ 45:5, 39:18, Matt 6:33).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the dispirited self-pitying servant; personal sorrow re-scaled by the age's sorrow; desire re-scaled ("seek not great things for yourself"); life itself as the sufficient gift. Chapter 45 tenderly corrects the weary Baruch — re-scaling his grief and his desire, and giving not greatness but *life* as the sufficient reward.
- **Book-level note (Jeremiah batch 7, chs 34–45, the narrative of the fall):** the scenes anatomise the interior under collapse: the *reneged repentance* (34); the Rechabites' *sustained faithfulness* shaming disobedience (35); the *word burned yet indestructible* and the *unmoved vs trembling* heart (36); the *suffering prophet*, the *outsider's compassion*, and the *fearful king who knows but will not act* (37-38); the *rescuer rescued because he trusted* (39); *generous trust betrayed* (40-41); *counterfeit guidance-seeking* by a pre-decided heart (42-43); the *fully defiant heart inverting cause and effect* (44); and the *dispirited servant re-scaled* and given his life (45). Master-findings: **a good act begun must be completed, not reneged**; **the gravest state is to hear God's word and feel no tremor**; **God rewards the trust behind the deed**; **counterfeit submission is exposed by the unwelcome answer**; and **discouragement is healed by re-scaling desire and receiving 'your life' as enough.**
- **Threads carried forward:** the trembling vs unmoved heart (Isa 66:2); trust rewarded (39:18; Heb 11:6); counterfeit seeking (Luke 6:46); "seek not great things" (Matt 6:33).

---

## Jer 46 - inner-being reading

# Jeremiah 46 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch8-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*. (Chs 46–51 = the oracles against the nations — largely *external-pole* judgment; the inner-being yield centres on *pride/false-trust judged* and God's word to his own servant.)

---

## JER-fear-not-jacob · Jeremiah 46:1–28 · [D, multi] — fear not amid the nations' judgment; measured discipline

**The reading.** The oracles against the nations open with Egypt, whose reliance is misplaced — judgment falls on "**Pharaoh… and those who trust in him**" (v.25). But the section turns, at its close, to God's own people with a tender reassurance: "**Fear not, O Jacob my servant… for I am with you… I will make a full end of all the nations to which I have driven you, but of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure, and I will by no means leave you unpunished**" (vv.27–28). The finding is **the servant told "**fear not… I am with you**" *while the nations fall* — his discipline "in just measure", never a "full end"** *(stated)*. The operation is **the interior of God's people *distinguished* from the nations in the very midst of universal judgment: the nations trusting Pharaoh come to a "full end", but of Jacob God will "not make a full end" — his correction is *measured* ("in just measure") and *preserving*, not destroying; so the servant, amid the collapse of everything, is told to "**fear not**" on the ground of God's *presence* ("I am with you")** *(inferred: the placement is the point — after chapters of judgment on the nations, God addresses *his own servant* with "**fear not**" (vv.27–28, repeating 30:10–11): the finding is that the same God whose judgment makes "a full end of all the nations" makes *no* full end of his people — the interior that belongs to God is *not consumed* in the general reckoning, because its discipline is *different in kind* (correction "in just measure", not destruction); and the ground of the servant's fearlessness amid universal collapse is *presence* — "**I am with you**": the finding is that when everything trusted-in falls (Egypt, the nations), the servant's security is not in any surviving structure but in *God's accompanying presence*, which distinguishes measured discipline from annihilation and grounds the "fear not")*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the servant distinguished from the nations in judgment ("of all the nations I will make a full end, but of you I will not" — the interior belonging to God not consumed in the general reckoning)* (thread — a gem: God's discipline of his own differs in kind from destruction, w/ 46:28, 30:11, Mal 3:17-18, Rom 8:1); *measured discipline, not annihilation ("I will discipline you in just measure" — correction preserving, never a full end)* (thread — a gem: severity proportioned within a keeping love, w/ 46:28, 10:24, 30:11); *"fear not, for I am with you" amid universal collapse (security in God's presence when everything trusted-in falls)* (thread — a gem: the servant's fearlessness grounded in accompaniment, not surviving structures, w/ 46:27-28, Isa 41:10, 43:1-2).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the servant distinguished from the nations in judgment; measured discipline, not annihilation; "fear not, for I am with you" amid universal collapse. Chapter 46 opens the nations-oracles by distinguishing God's servant — "fear not… I am with you… of you I will not make a full end" — his discipline measured, never destroying.
- **Threads:** "fear not" / measured discipline (← 30:10-11; w/ Isa 41:10); the servant distinguished (w/ Mal 3:17-18); misplaced trust in the nations (← Isa 31:1; 46:25).

---

## Jer 47 - inner-being reading

# Jeremiah 47–49 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch8-v1-20260704`). Cross-chapter (47:1–49:39), filed at anchor. Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-nations-pride · Jeremiah 47:1–49:39 · [D, multi] — complacency, false trust, and self-deceiving pride judged; God's grief even for the judged

**The reading.** The oracles against Moab, Ammon, Edom, and the rest anatomise the *interiors* behind the nations. Moab's sin is *undisturbed complacency*: "**Moab has been at ease from his youth and has settled on his dregs; he has not been emptied from vessel to vessel… so his taste remains in him**" (48:11); and *pride*: "**We have heard of the pride of Moab… his loftiness, his pride, and his arrogance, and the haughtiness of his heart… his boasts are false**" (48:29–30). Ammon *trusts its wealth*: "**who trusted in her treasures, saying, 'Who will come against me?'**" (49:4). Edom is *self-deceived by pride*: "**The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who live in the clefts of the rock… Though you make your nest as high as the eagle's, I will bring you down**" (49:16). Yet God's heart is not cold: "**my heart moans for Moab like a flute**" (48:36), and to Ammon's orphans: "**Leave your fatherless children; I will keep them alive; and let your widows trust in me**" (49:11). The finding is **the nations' interiors judged — *complacency* ("settled on his dregs"), *false trust* in wealth ("who will come against me?"), and *self-deceiving pride* ("the pride of your heart has deceived you") — yet met with God's *grief* ("my heart moans") and *care* for the vulnerable ("let your widows trust in me")** *(stated)*. The operation is **three recurring disorders of the interior, drawn from the nations but universal: (1) *complacency undisturbed* — Moab "**settled on his dregs**, not emptied from vessel to vessel", the self that has never been *shaken* and so has grown stale and self-satisfied; (2) *false security in wealth* — "who will come against me?", the self walled by its treasures into a false invulnerability; (3) *self-deceiving pride* — "the pride of your heart **has deceived you**", the loftiness that *lies to itself* about its unassailability (as Obadiah); and against all three, God's *grief* over the judged and his *care* for their weak** *(inferred: the Moab wine-image (48:11) is a striking inner-being figure — "**settled on his dregs** (lees)… not emptied from vessel to vessel, so his taste remains": wine left undisturbed on its sediment grows *thick and stale*; the finding is that a life *never shaken* — "at ease from his youth", never "emptied", never disturbed by adversity or exile — becomes *complacent and coarse*, its "taste unchanged" (untransformed); the finding is that *undisturbed ease* is not a blessing but a danger to the interior, which needs to be "poured from vessel to vessel" (shaken, moved, tested) to be refined; (2) the false trust "**who will come against me?**" (49:4) and Edom's "make your nest high as the eagle's" (49:16) name the *illusion of invulnerability* that wealth and height breed — the same self-deceiving pride of Obadiah; and (3) the most searching note is God's *grief* — "**my heart moans for Moab like a flute**" (48:36): the finding is that God's judgment on the proud nations is not gleeful but *grieved* — even as he judges Moab's arrogance his heart "moans" for it (as Jeremiah wept over Judah); and his *care* extends to the enemy's vulnerable — "**let your widows trust in me**" (49:11): the finding is that God's compassion reaches the weak even among the judged nations — the fatherless and widows of Ammon are invited to trust him; so the oracles judge the proud interior while disclosing a God who grieves over the judged and shelters their weak)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *complacency undisturbed ("Moab at ease from his youth, settled on his dregs, not emptied from vessel to vessel" — the unshaken life grown stale and self-satisfied, its taste untransformed)* (new — a gem: undisturbed ease a danger; the interior needs shaking to be refined, w/ 48:11, Zeph 1:12, Ps 55:19, Amos 6:1); *false security in wealth and height ("who trusted in her treasures, Who will come against me?"; "make your nest high as the eagle's" — the illusion of invulnerability)* (thread — a gem: wealth and elevation breeding false unassailability, w/ 49:4,16, Obad 3-4, Prov 18:11); *self-deceiving pride ("the pride of your heart has deceived you" — loftiness that lies to itself)* (thread — a gem: pride distorting self-perception, w/ 49:16, Obad 3, Jer 17:9); *God's grief over the judged ("my heart moans for Moab like a flute" — judgment grieved, not gleeful)* (thread — a gem: God grieving even the proud he judges, w/ 48:36, 9:1, Isa 16:11, Ezek 33:11); *care for the enemy's vulnerable ("let your widows trust in me" — compassion reaching the weak among the judged)* (new — w/ 49:11, Ps 68:5).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** complacency undisturbed; false security in wealth and height; self-deceiving pride; God's grief over the judged; care for the enemy's vulnerable. Chapters 47–49 judge the nations' interiors — stale complacency, false trust, and self-deceiving pride — while disclosing a God who *grieves* over the judged and shelters their weak.
- **Threads:** undisturbed complacency (→ Zeph 1:12; Amos 6:1); self-deceiving pride (← Obad 3-4; Jer 17:9; 49:16); God's grief over the judged (← 9:1; Ezek 33:11); care for the vulnerable (w/ Ps 68:5).

---

## Jer 50 - inner-being reading

# Jeremiah 50–51 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per oracle unit (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch8-v1-20260704`). Cross-chapter (50:1–51:64), filed at anchor. Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## JER-babylon-redeemer · Jeremiah 50:1–51:64 · [D, multi] — the proud judged; the strong Redeemer who pleads their cause; sins sought and none found

**The reading.** The long oracle against Babylon indicts her *pride against God*: "**she has been proud against the LORD**" (50:29); "**Behold, I am against you, O proud one… The proud one shall stumble and fall, with none to raise him up**" (50:31–32); "**Though Babylon should mount up to heaven… destroyers would come from me against her**" (51:53). Set against Babylon's fall is a stunning word of grace to God's own people: "**In those days… iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none, and sin in Judah, and none shall be found, for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant**" (50:20); and "**Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name. He will surely plead their cause**" (50:34); "**Let not your heart faint**" (51:46). The finding is **the *proud self-exalting* power judged ("mount up to heaven… I am against you, O proud one") — against a people whose sins, when *sought, cannot be found* ("there shall be none"), because their "**Redeemer is strong**" and *pleads their cause*** *(stated)*. The operation is **two interiors and two outcomes: the *self-exalting* (Babylon "mounting up to heaven", "proud against the LORD") that God is "against" and that "stumbles with none to raise it"; and the *redeemed*, whose guilt has been so *thoroughly dealt with* that when God himself "seeks" for it, "**there shall be none**" — the sin not merely covered but *removed past finding*, because a "**strong Redeemer**" has "pleaded their cause"** *(inferred: the Babylon-judgment reprises the archetype of pride (self-exaltation "to heaven", 51:53, as Isa 14) — the finding is that the God-usurping interior, however high it climbs, is the one God is "**against**" and that falls "with none to raise it up" (50:32); but the inner-being jewel is 50:20 — "**iniquity shall be SOUGHT in Israel, and there shall be NONE… for I will pardon**": the finding is a picture of forgiveness so complete that the guilt is *un-findable* — not that the sin never was, but that when God *searches* for it (the God who "searches the heart", 17:10), it is *gone*, "none shall be found" (the same as "remember their sin no more", 31:34); the interior stands before the all-seeing God with its record *not merely forgiven but erased past discovery*; and the ground is 50:34 — "**their Redeemer is STRONG… he will surely PLEAD THEIR CAUSE**": the finding is that this un-findable forgiveness rests on a *Redeemer* (go'el — the kinsman who buys back and defends) who is *strong* enough to make good the redemption and who *acts as their advocate* ("pleads their cause") — so the erasure of guilt is not the interior's achievement but the work of a mighty Redeemer who takes their case as his own; the contrast is total: the proud who exalt themselves fall un-raised, while the redeemed whose cause a strong Redeemer pleads stand with no sin to be found)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the self-exalting power judged ("proud against the LORD… though Babylon mount up to heaven… I am against you, O proud one" — the God-usurping interior God is against, falling with none to raise it)* (thread — a gem: self-exaltation, however high, the thing God opposes, w/ 50:29,31-32, 51:53, Isa 14:13-15, Jas 4:6); *forgiveness so complete the sin cannot be found ("iniquity shall be sought in Israel and there shall be none… for I will pardon" — guilt erased past discovery, not merely covered)* (thread — a gem: the interior standing before the all-seeing God with its record un-findable, w/ 50:20, 31:34, Isa 43:25, Ps 103:12, Rom 8:33-34); *the strong Redeemer who pleads their cause ("their Redeemer is strong… he will surely plead their cause" — the erasure of guilt the work of a mighty Advocate, not the self)* (new — a gem: the go'el strong enough to redeem and acting as advocate, w/ 50:34, Job 19:25, Isa 47:4, 1 John 2:1); *"let not your heart faint" (the redeemed steadied amid the turmoil of the age)* (thread — w/ 51:46, Isa 7:4).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the self-exalting power judged; forgiveness so complete the sin cannot be found; the strong Redeemer who pleads their cause; "let not your heart faint". Chapters 50–51 set proud, heaven-climbing Babylon (whom God is "against") beside the redeemed whose sins, when sought, "shall be none" — because their "Redeemer is strong" and pleads their cause.
- **Threads:** self-exaltation judged (← Isa 14:13; Jer 49:16; w/ Jas 4:6); sin sought and none found (← 31:34; w/ Isa 43:25, Rom 8:33-34); the strong Redeemer (w/ Job 19:25, 1 John 2:1).

---

## Jer 52 - inner-being reading

# Jeremiah 52 — inner-being scene reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per scene (provenance `jeremiah-oracle-segmentation-batch8-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*. (Ch.52 is a historical *appendix* recounting the fall; its inner-being yield is the closing note of kindness.)

---

## JER-jehoiachin-kindness · Jeremiah 52:1–34 · [D, multi] — the fall recorded; the closing note of kindness and hope

**The reading.** The book's appendix recounts the fall in sober detail — the siege, the famine, the breaching of the walls, the burning of the temple, the exile (vv.4–30). But the very last paragraph, where the long book of judgment ends, turns unexpectedly gentle: after thirty-seven years in prison, the exiled king Jehoiachin is released — "**and he spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat above the seats of the kings who were with him in Babylon. So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments, and every day of his life he dined regularly at the king's table**" (vv.32–33). The finding is **the vast book of judgment closing not on the fire of the temple but on a *small, quiet kindness* — the imprisoned king lifted up, re-clothed, and fed "every day of his life"** *(stated)*. The operation is **the deliberate *placement* of a tender mercy at the book's very end: after all the wrath, the last word is *grace* — a prisoner released, "**spoken kindly to**", raised above his fellow-kings, his "prison garments" put off, given daily bread; the interior meaning is that the story of judgment does not end in judgment but leaves a *seed of hope*** *(inferred: the appendix could have ended with the burning temple and the exile (v.30) — but the book's final paragraph is *chosen* to be Jehoiachin's release (vv.31–34); the finding is that this placement is itself the message — after fifty-one chapters weighted toward wrath, the *last note* is *kindness*: a prisoner of thirty-seven years "**spoken kindly to**", his prison clothes exchanged, "**every day of his life**" fed at the king's table; the finding is that the God whose judgment the book records leaves, at the very end, a *seed of grace and hope* — the Davidic king, though in exile, is *lifted and sustained*, so the line is not extinguished and the future is not closed; the "prison garments put off" (v.33) quietly echoes the re-clothing of grace (as Joshua's filthy garments, Zech 3; the prodigal's robe), and the "every day" of provision speaks of a sustaining mercy that outlasts the judgment; the finding is that the interior is left, after all the darkness, with *hope* — the book of the fall ends with a released king at a king's table, a small light held out past the catastrophe)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *judgment closing on kindness, not wrath (the long book of the fall ending on Jehoiachin's release, "spoken kindly to", re-clothed, fed "every day of his life")* (new — a gem: the deliberate placement of a tender mercy as the last word, w/ 52:31-34, Lam 3:22, Hab 3:2); *the seed of hope preserved (the Davidic king lifted and sustained in exile — the line not extinguished, the future not closed)* (new — a gem: a small light held out past the catastrophe, w/ 52:31-34, 2 Kgs 25:27-30, Jer 33:17); *re-clothing and daily provision as grace ("put off his prison garments… every day of his life dined at the king's table")* (thread — sustaining mercy imaged, w/ 52:33, Zech 3:4, Luke 15:22).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** judgment closing on kindness, not wrath; the seed of hope preserved; re-clothing and daily provision as grace. Chapter 52 ends the whole book of judgment on a *small, quiet mercy* — the imprisoned king released, spoken kindly to, re-clothed, and fed daily — a seed of hope held out past the catastrophe.
- **Book-level note (Jeremiah, chs 46–52):** the nations-oracles judge the *proud, complacent, self-secure* interior (stale Moab "settled on his dregs"; Ammon's "who will come against me?"; Edom's self-deceiving pride; Babylon "mounting up to heaven") while disclosing a God who *grieves* over the judged (48:36), *shelters* their vulnerable (49:11), *distinguishes and preserves* his own servant ("fear not… I am with you", 46:28), and provides a *strong Redeemer* whose pardon leaves the redeemed's sin *un-findable* (50:20,34) — and the whole book ends on a *kindness* (52). Master-findings: **undisturbed ease breeds a stale, self-satisfied interior**; **self-exalting pride is the thing God is 'against'**; **the redeemed's guilt, sought, cannot be found, for their Redeemer is strong**; and **judgment's last word is kindness.**
- **★ JEREMIAH COMPLETE** (52 chapters). The book's book-wide arc: from the *deceitful, un-turnable heart* forsaking the fountain for broken cisterns (2, 17) to the *new covenant* that writes the law within, makes God known, and remembers sin no more (31) — the interior God cannot mend from outside, remade from within by grace, and kept by a strong Redeemer.
- **Threads:** self-exalting pride (Isa 14; Jer 50:31); sin un-findable / new covenant (31:34, 50:20); the strong Redeemer (Job 19:25); judgment ending in mercy (Lam 3:22).

---

## Eze 1 - inner-being reading

# Ezekiel 1 — inner-being vision reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per vision-unit (provenance `ezekiel-segmentation-batch1-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## EZE-glory-vision · Ezekiel 1:1–28 · [D, multi] — the overwhelming vision of God's glory that prostrates the seer

**The reading.** By the Chebar canal among the exiles, "**the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God**" (v.1). An immense, mobile, many-eyed apparatus of living creatures and wheels-within-wheels rises, and above it all "**the likeness of a throne… and seated above the likeness of a throne was a likeness with a human appearance**" (v.26), wrapped in rainbow brightness — "**Such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard the voice of one speaking**" (v.28). The finding is **the encounter with the *glory of the LORD* that *prostrates* the seer — "when I saw it, I fell on my face"** *(stated)*. The operation is **the interior *undone* by the vision of transcendent glory — the involuntary collapse ("fell on my face") that the sight of God's majesty produces, and the disclosure that God's glory reaches his people *even in exile* ("by the Chebar canal", in Babylon), not confined to the temple** *(inferred: the whole cascade of imagery (creatures, wheels, eyes, crystal, fire, rainbow) piles up to overwhelm — and its effect on the interior is a single involuntary act: "**I fell on my face**" (v.28); the finding is that the true sight of God's *glory* (kavod — weight, majesty) does not elate but *floors* the beholder — the appropriate reflex of the creature before the Holy is prostration (as Isa 6:5, Dan 8:17, Rev 1:17); the elaborate "likeness… appearance… likeness" language (Ezekiel never says he saw God directly, only "the *likeness* of the glory") registers a further inner-being note — the seer is careful not to overclaim, awed into *reticence* before the ungraspable; and the *location* matters — this glory appears "**among the exiles by the Chebar canal**" (vv.1,3), in unclean Babylon far from the temple: the finding is that God's glory is *not confined* to the holy place — it comes to his people in their displacement, so the exile is not beyond the reach of the God whose throne is *mobile* (the wheels), able to go where his people are)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the glory that prostrates ("when I saw it, I fell on my face" — the sight of God's majesty flooring the beholder, prostration the creature's reflex before the Holy)* (thread — a gem: true sight of glory undoes rather than elates, w/ 1:28, Isa 6:5, Dan 8:17, Rev 1:17); *awed reticence before the ungraspable (the careful "likeness… appearance" language — the seer not overclaiming)* (new — reverent restraint before what cannot be grasped, w/ 1:26-28, Exod 33:20); *God's glory not confined to the holy place ("visions of God… by the Chebar canal" in exile — the mobile throne reaching his people in displacement)* (new — a gem: God's presence coming to the exiled, not bound to the temple, w/ 1:1-3, 11:16, Ps 139:7-10).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the glory that prostrates; awed reticence before the ungraspable; God's glory not confined to the holy place. Chapter 1 opens Ezekiel with the overwhelming vision of God's mobile glory reaching the exiles — a sight that floors the seer on his face.
- **Threads:** the glory / prostration (→ 3:23, 8-11 the departing glory, 43 the returning glory; w/ Isa 6:5); God's presence in exile (→ 11:16); the encounter that undoes (w/ Dan 8:17, 10:8).

---

## Eze 2 - inner-being reading

# Ezekiel 2–3 — inner-being scene reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per unit (provenance `ezekiel-segmentation-batch1-v1-20260704`). Cross-chapter (2:1–3:15), filed at anchor. Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## EZE-eat-the-scroll · Ezekiel 2:1–3:15 · [D, multi] — the word internalised (sweet though full of woe); the hardened face given; the cost of bearing it

**The reading.** Raised to his feet by the Spirit, Ezekiel is sent to "**a rebellious house… impudent and stubborn**" (2:3–4) with the charge, "**be not afraid of them, nor be dismayed at their looks**" (2:6). He is handed a scroll "**written on the front and on the back… words of lamentation and mourning and woe**" (2:10) and told to *eat* it: "**Son of man, feed your belly with this scroll… Then I ate it, and it was in my mouth as sweet as honey**" (3:3). For the hard-faced audience God gives him a matching hardness: "**I have made your forehead… like emery harder than flint**" (3:9), and bids him "**receive [my words] in your heart**" (3:10). The bearing of it costs him: "**I went in bitterness in the heat of my spirit… and I sat there overwhelmed among them seven days**" (3:14–15). The finding is **the word of God *eaten* — internalised so wholly it becomes part of the self, and *sweet* even though its content is "lamentation and woe" — with a *hardened face* given for a hard audience, and a real *bitterness and overwhelming* in bearing it** *(stated)*. The operation is **the prophet's interior *formed by the word*: he does not merely *carry* a message but *eats* it — takes it *inside*, into "belly" and "heart" — so that the word becomes his own substance; and the paradox that the word is *sweet* to taste (the delight of receiving God's own word, as Jer 15:16) even though its message is *woe*; and the equipping — a "forehead harder than flint" *given* to match the stubborn faces he must confront; and the honest *cost* — even so equipped, he goes "in bitterness" and sits "overwhelmed" for seven days** *(inferred: the *eating* of the scroll (3:1–3) is the inner-being center — the finding is that God's word is meant to be *internalised*, not merely handled: Ezekiel *ingests* it ("feed your belly… fill your stomach"), so it passes *into* him and becomes part of who he is — the messenger must first be *inwardly filled* with the word before he can speak it; and the *sweetness* is a striking note — "**as sweet as honey**" (3:3) though the scroll's content is "lamentation and mourning and woe" (2:10): the finding is that *receiving God's word is itself sweet* — a delight to the one who loves God — even when the word's *message* is grievous; the sweetness is in the *word as God's* (the intimacy of being given his very words), not in its cheerful content (as Jer 15:16, "your words became the delight of my heart"; yet cf. Rev 10:10, sweet in the mouth, bitter in the belly); and the *hardened forehead* (3:8–9) is grace for the task — God does not send the sensitive prophet defenceless against "briers, thorns, scorpions" but *makes his face hard* to match theirs, an equipping of resolve; yet the honesty of 3:14–15 completes it — even the God-hardened, word-filled prophet goes "**in BITTERNESS**… OVERWHELMED seven days": the finding is that bearing God's heavy word is *genuinely costly* — the equipping does not remove the grief; the prophet is sweet-fed and flint-faced and *still* bitter and overwhelmed, the interior carrying a weight that the calling does not lighten)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the word internalised, eaten ("eat this scroll… feed your belly… receive my words in your heart" — the messenger inwardly filled with the word before speaking it)* (thread — a gem: God's word ingested, becoming the self's substance, not merely handled, w/ 3:1-3,10, Jer 15:16, Ps 119:11, Col 3:16); *the word sweet though its message is woe ("words of lamentation and woe"… "sweet as honey" — receiving God's word itself sweet even when grievous)* (new — a gem: the sweetness in the word as God's, not in its content, w/ 2:10/3:3, Jer 15:16, Rev 10:9-10, Ps 19:10); *the hardened face given for the task ("your forehead like emery harder than flint" — resolve equipped by God to match the stubborn audience)* (new — a gem: God hardening the sensitive messenger for the hard hearers, w/ 3:8-9, Isa 50:7, Jer 1:18); *the real cost of bearing the word ("I went in bitterness… overwhelmed seven days" — the grief the equipping does not remove)* (thread — a gem: the sweet-fed, flint-faced prophet still bitter and overwhelmed, w/ 3:14-15, Jer 20:9,14, Dan 8:27).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the word internalised; the word sweet though its message is woe; the hardened face given; the real cost of bearing the word. Chapters 2–3 form the prophet by the word — eaten and made his own substance, sweet even in its woe, his face hardened for the task, yet leaving him bitter and overwhelmed.
- **Threads:** the word internalised / eaten (← Jer 15:16; w/ Rev 10:9-10, Ps 119:11); the hardened face (w/ Isa 50:7, Jer 1:18); the cost of the word (← Jer 20:9; → Eze 24); the rebellious house / hard heart (→ 3:7, 11:19).

---

## Eze 3 - inner-being reading

# Ezekiel 3 — inner-being scene reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per unit (provenance `ezekiel-segmentation-batch1-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## EZE-watchman · Ezekiel 3:16–27 · [D, multi] — the watchman's responsibility; delivering one's own soul by warning; the bound and mute prophet

**The reading.** After seven days God commissions Ezekiel afresh: "**I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me**" (v.17). The charge is weighted with *responsibility*: if the watchman fails to warn the wicked, "**that wicked person shall die for his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand**" (v.18); but "**if you warn the wicked, and he does not turn… he shall die for his iniquity, but you will have delivered your soul**" (v.19). Then, strangely, God binds him and makes him *mute* — "**I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, so that you shall be mute**" — until "**when I speak with you, I will open your mouth**" (vv.26–27). The finding is **the *watchman's charge* — accountable to *warn*, so that failing to warn makes him *bloodguilty*, while warning *delivers his own soul* (regardless of the hearer's response) — and the *mute* prophet who speaks only when God opens his mouth** *(stated)*. The operation is **the interior burdened with *responsibility for warning others*: the watchman is answerable not for whether they *heed* but for whether he *warns* — his own soul is "delivered" by faithful warning even if the hearer perishes, and imperilled ("blood required at your hand") by silence; and the paradox of the *mute* prophet — bound and speechless *except* when God gives the word — locating the whole authority of his speech in God's initiative** *(inferred: the watchman-image (vv.17–21) defines a specific inner-being weight — *responsibility for the warning, not the outcome*: the finding is that the one who knows God's word is *accountable to speak it* — his "soul is delivered" (v.19) by *faithfully warning*, whether or not the hearer turns; the result is God's and the hearer's, but the *warning* is the watchman's charge, and *silence* makes him complicit in the death he could have spoken against ("his blood I will require at your hand"); the finding is that to know a saving truth and withhold it is a grave failure, while to speak it faithfully *clears* one's own conscience even when it is rejected — the responsibility is *to warn*, and it is discharged by warning; and the strange muteness (vv.26–27) adds a counter-weight — the watchman who is bidden to speak is also made *unable to speak* except when God opens his mouth: the finding is that the prophet's authority is *entirely derivative* — he does not speak at will but *only God's given word*, so his silence and his speech are both under God's hand; the interior is thus held in tension — *bound* to warn yet *bound* from speaking his own words, answerable to declare God's word and forbidden to substitute his own)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the watchman accountable to warn, not for the outcome ("if you give no warning… his blood I will require at your hand; if you warn… you will have delivered your soul" — responsible for the warning, the result God's and the hearer's)* (thread — a gem: to know a saving truth and withhold it is grave failure; faithful warning clears the conscience even when rejected, w/ 3:17-21, 33:1-9, Acts 20:26-27, 1 Cor 9:16); *delivering one's own soul by faithfulness regardless of response (the watchman's soul secured by warning, not by success)* (new — a gem: faithfulness, not results, discharges the charge, w/ 3:19,21, Ezek 33:9); *the derivative authority of the mute prophet ("mute… until I open your mouth" — speaking only God's given word, not his own)* (new — a gem: the prophet bound to warn yet bound from his own words, authority wholly derivative, w/ 3:26-27, Num 22:38, John 12:49).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the watchman accountable to warn, not for the outcome; delivering one's own soul by faithfulness regardless of response; the derivative authority of the mute prophet. Chapter 3 lays the watchman's charge — answerable to *warn* (his soul delivered by faithfulness, imperilled by silence) — and makes him mute except when God gives the word.
- **Book-level note (Ezekiel batch 1, chs 1–3):** the call joins three inner-being fields — the *glory that prostrates* the seer (1), the *word internalised* (eaten, sweet-though-woeful, borne at real cost) and the *hardened face* given for a hard people (2–3:15), and the *watchman's responsibility* to warn (3:16-27). Master-findings: **the sight of God's glory floors the beholder**; **the messenger must first eat the word — take it inside — and even so bears it at cost**; and **to know God's word is to be accountable to warn, delivering one's soul by faithfulness, not results.**
- **Threads:** the glory (← 1:28; → 8-11, 43); the word eaten (← 2:8-3:3); the watchman (→ 33:1-9); the prophet's cost (← 3:14; → 24).

---

## Eze 4 - inner-being reading

# Ezekiel 4–7 — inner-being scene reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per unit (provenance `ezekiel-segmentation-batch2-v1-20260704`). Cross-chapter (4:1–7:27), filed at anchor. Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## EZE-sign-siege · Ezekiel 4:1–7:27 · [D, multi] — the prophet's body made a sign; un-pitying justice; God broken over the whoring heart

**The reading.** Ezekiel is made to *enact* the siege in his own body — an iron griddle set as a wall, cords binding him so "**you cannot turn from one side to the other**" (4:8), siege-rations eaten in the city's sight. The judgment oracles are severe: "**my eye will not spare you, nor will I have pity**" (7:4,9); "**I, even I, am against you**" (5:8). Yet within the severity a wound is disclosed — the survivors "**will remember me among the nations… how I have been broken over their whoring heart that has departed from me, and over their eyes that go whoring after their idols**" (6:9). The finding is **the prophet's *body made a message* (bound, bearing the siege), God's *un-pitying justice* ("my eye will not spare"), and beneath it God's *grief* — "**I have been broken over their whoring heart**"** *(stated)*. The operation is **two inner-being disclosures: the prophet whose *very body is conscripted* into the message (his physical constraint and privation *are* the sermon), and — most importantly — the *wounded love beneath the severe justice*: God's "eye will not spare", yet he says he "**has been BROKEN**" over the heart that left him, so the unsparing judgment is the act of a God who is himself *heartbroken* by the unfaithfulness** *(inferred: the sign-acts (4:1–8) make the prophet's *body* the medium — bound with cords, immobile, eating measured rations: the finding is that the message can require the *whole self*, not just the voice — Ezekiel's constrained, suffering body *is* the word, the calling reaching into his physical existence (as ch.24 will demand even his grief); and the severe refrain "**my eye will not spare, nor will I have pity**" (5:11, 7:4,9) could seem to portray a merciless God — but 6:9 pierces that reading: "**how I HAVE BEEN BROKEN over their WHORING HEART**" (the God who judges is the God who is *wounded* — "broken", shavar, shattered — by the heart's departure); the finding is that God's unsparing justice is not cold cruelty but the severity of a *betrayed lover* — his "eye will not spare" precisely because his heart has been "broken" by the "whoring heart that has departed from me"; the image is marital (whoring), so the judgment is the anguish of a spouse betrayed, not the indifference of a tyrant; and the goal even of the severity is *recognition and remembrance* — "then they will REMEMBER me" (6:9): the finding is that the wounded God's judgment aims to bring the straying heart back to *remember* the One it left)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the whole self conscripted into the message (the prophet's bound, suffering body made the sermon)* (thread — a gem: the calling reaching into physical existence, the body itself the word, w/ 4:1-8, 24:16-24, Hos 1-3, Isa 20:2-4); *un-pitying justice as the severity of wounded love ("my eye will not spare"… "I have been broken over their whoring heart" — the judging God himself heartbroken by the betrayal)* (thread — a gem: God's severity the anguish of a betrayed lover, not the indifference of a tyrant, w/ 5:11/6:9, Hos 11:8, Jer 3:20, Isa 63:9-10); *the aim of judgment is remembrance ("then they will remember me… how I have been broken" — the severity meant to bring the straying heart back to remember)* (new — a gem: judgment aiming at the return of the heart, w/ 6:9, Luke 15:17-18); *the whoring heart departed (the interior's unfaithfulness figured as adultery)* (thread — w/ 6:9, Jer 3, Hos 2).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the whole self conscripted into the message; un-pitying justice as the severity of wounded love; the aim of judgment is remembrance; the whoring heart departed. Chapters 4–7 make the prophet's *body* the sermon and disclose, beneath the unsparing justice, a God "broken over their whoring heart" — severity as the anguish of a betrayed love aiming to bring the heart back.
- **Threads:** the body as sign (→ 24:16-24; w/ Hos 1-3); wounded love beneath judgment (← Hos 11:8, Isa 63:9; → Eze 6:9); the whoring heart / new heart (→ 11:19, 36:26).

---

## Eze 8 - inner-being reading

# Ezekiel 8–9 — inner-being scene reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per unit (provenance `ezekiel-segmentation-batch2-v1-20260704`). Cross-chapter (8:1–9:11), filed at anchor. Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## EZE-lord-does-not-see · Ezekiel 8:1–9:11 · [D, multi] — the hidden idolatry that thinks God unseeing; the mark on those who sigh and groan

**The reading.** Carried in vision to the temple, Ezekiel is shown *escalating* secret abominations: idols "**engraved on the wall all around**" (8:10), and the elders worshipping them "**in the dark, each in his room of pictures**", saying, "**The LORD does not see us, the LORD has forsaken the land**" (8:12); then twenty-five men "**with their backs to the temple**" worshipping the sun (8:16). Then judgment, preceded by a rescue: a man in linen is sent to "**put a mark on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations that are committed in it**" (9:4) — and the slaughter is to "**touch no one on whom is the mark**", beginning "**at my sanctuary**" (9:6). Ezekiel intercedes: "**Ah, Lord GOD! Will you destroy all the remnant?**" (9:8). The finding is **the *hidden idolatry* of hearts that think "**the LORD does not see us**" — and the *mark* set on those who "**sigh and groan**" over the abominations, distinguishing the grieving remnant** *(stated)*. The operation is **two contrasting interiors: the one that practises its idolatry *"in the dark"* on the *conviction that God does not see* ("the LORD does not see us… has forsaken the land") — a practical atheism that emboldens secret sin; and the one that *grieves* over the same abominations — and it is precisely this *grief over sin* ("sigh and groan") that God *marks* for sparing, so the interior that still *feels the wrongness* is the saved one** *(inferred: 8:12 exposes a specific inner-being corruption — idolatry practised "**in the dark, each in his room of pictures**", justified by "**the LORD does not see us**": the finding is that hidden sin rests on a *practical atheism* — the (false) conviction that God is *not watching* ("has forsaken the land"), which *emboldens* the heart to do in secret what it would not do in the open; the "room of pictures" is the *chamber of the imagination*, the private interior gallery of one's idols, indulged where one believes no eye sees (the opposite of "no hiding from the God who fills all", Jer 23:24); and the counter-interior of 9:4 is the inner-being jewel — those *marked for sparing* are "**those who SIGH AND GROAN over all the abominations**": the finding is that the mark of the saved is *grief over the surrounding evil* — not activism or perfection but the *inward mourning* that still feels sin's wrongness when everyone else is numb; the ones spared are those whose consciences are not seared, who "sigh and groan" over what others do "in the dark"; and the judgment "**beginning at my sanctuary**" (9:6) with the elders adds that accountability starts with the religious leadership; Ezekiel's intercession (9:8) shows the prophet's heart still pleading for the remnant even as judgment falls)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *hidden idolatry on the conviction God does not see ("in the dark… the LORD does not see us" — practical atheism emboldening secret sin)* (thread — a gem: hidden sin resting on the false belief that God is not watching, the private chamber of the imagination's idols, w/ 8:12, 9:9, Jer 23:24, Ps 10:11, 94:7); *the room of pictures (the interior gallery of one's idols indulged where one thinks no eye sees)* (new — a gem: the private imagination as the secret shrine, w/ 8:10-12, Matt 5:28); *the mark of grief over sin ("those who sigh and groan over all the abominations" — the spared are those whose consciences still mourn the surrounding evil)* (new — a gem: inward grief over sin, not activism or perfection, the mark of the saved when others are numb, w/ 9:4, 2 Pet 2:7-8, Ps 119:136); *the interceding prophet ("will you destroy all the remnant?" — the heart still pleading amid judgment)* (thread — w/ 9:8, 11:13, Amos 7:2).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** hidden idolatry on the conviction God does not see; the room of pictures; the mark of grief over sin; the interceding prophet. Chapters 8–9 contrast the heart that sins "in the dark" believing "the LORD does not see" with the heart that "sighs and groans" over the abominations — and it is the *grieving* interior that God marks to spare.
- **Threads:** God unseeing / hidden sin (← Jer 23:24, Ps 94:7); the imagination's idols (w/ Matt 5:28); grief over sin (→ 2 Pet 2:7-8, Ps 119:136); intercession (← 9:8; → 11:13).

---

## Eze 10 - inner-being reading

# Ezekiel 10–11 — inner-being vision reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per unit (provenance `ezekiel-segmentation-batch2-v1-20260704`). Cross-chapter (10:1–11:25), filed at anchor. Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## EZE-glory-departs-heart-of-flesh · Ezekiel 10:1–11:25 · [D, multi] — the glory withdrawing; God a sanctuary in exile; the heart of stone replaced by a heart of flesh

**The reading.** The vision Ezekiel most dreads unfolds in slow stages: "**the glory of the LORD went up from the cherub to the threshold of the house**" (10:4); then "**the glory of the LORD went out from the threshold… and stood over the cherubim**" (10:18); then it rose to "**the east gate**" (10:19); and finally "**the glory of the LORD went up from the midst of the city and stood on the mountain that is on the east side of the city**" (11:23) — God's presence *leaving* his temple by degrees. Yet a word of grace comes to the exiles: "**though I scattered them among the countries, yet I have been a sanctuary to them for a while in the countries where they have gone**" (11:16); and the great promise: "**I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh**" (11:19). The finding is **the *glory departing* the defiled temple by stages — yet God himself becoming "**a sanctuary**" to the exiles — and the promise to *replace the heart of stone with a heart of flesh*** *(stated)*. The operation is **the sober disclosure that God's presence *withdraws* from persistent defilement (the glory does not flee instantly but leaves *reluctantly, by stages*, as if grieving to go) — balanced by the astonishing grace that the departed glory does not *abandon* his people but becomes "**a sanctuary**" to them *in exile* (presence relocated from the building to the people); and the deepest promise, that the *hard, unfeeling heart* (the stone) will be *removed* and a *responsive, tender heart* (flesh) *given*** *(inferred: the *staged departure* of the glory (10:4,18,19; 11:23) is deliberately *slow* — threshold, cherubim, east gate, mountain: the finding is that God's presence *withdraws with reluctance*, lingering at each step as if loath to leave, so the departure itself testifies to a grieving love (he does not slam the door but backs away step by step); and yet — crucially — the withdrawal is *not abandonment*: "**I have been a SANCTUARY to them… in the countries where they have gone**" (11:16): the finding is that when the *building* is defiled and forsaken, God himself becomes the *sanctuary* — his presence relocated from the temple to the *people* wherever they are (the seed of "the temple is his people", the presence not bound to a place, as ch.1's mobile throne showed); and the summit is 11:19 — "**a HEART OF STONE… a HEART OF FLESH**": the finding is Ezekiel's parallel to Jeremiah's new covenant — the fundamental problem is a *heart of stone* (hard, unfeeling, unresponsive to God), and the fundamental remedy is *transplant*, not repair — God *removes* the stone heart and *gives* a heart of "flesh" (soft, tender, responsive), along with "one heart" (undivided) and "a new spirit"; the finding is that the interior's decisive transformation is *received, not achieved* — the stone cannot soften itself; God must give the new heart)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the glory withdrawing by reluctant stages (threshold, cherubim, east gate, mountain — God's presence leaving persistent defilement slowly, as if grieving to go)* (thread — a gem: the reluctant departure testifying to a grieving love, w/ 10:4,18-19, 11:23, Hos 11:8); *God himself a sanctuary in exile ("I have been a sanctuary to them… in the countries where they have gone" — presence relocated from the building to the people)* (new — a gem: the presence not bound to a place, God the sanctuary of the scattered, w/ 11:16, 1:1-3, John 4:21-24); *the heart of stone replaced by a heart of flesh ("I will remove the heart of stone… and give them a heart of flesh" — the hard unresponsive heart transplanted, not repaired)* (thread — a gem, Ezekiel's parallel to the new covenant: the decisive transformation received, not achieved; the stone cannot soften itself, w/ 11:19, 36:26, Jer 31:33, 2 Cor 3:3); *"one heart and a new spirit" (the undivided, God-given interior)* (thread — w/ 11:19, 36:26).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the glory withdrawing by reluctant stages; God himself a sanctuary in exile; the heart of stone replaced by a heart of flesh; "one heart and a new spirit". Chapters 10–11 show the glory *leaving* the defiled temple by grieving degrees — yet God becoming a *sanctuary* to the exiles, and promising to transplant the heart of stone for a heart of flesh.
- **Book-level note (Ezekiel batch 2, chs 4–11):** the movement joins *judgment enacted and grieved* with the *seed of the great promise*. Its findings: the prophet's *body made the sermon* and God's *un-pitying justice* revealed as *wounded love* ("broken over their whoring heart", 6:9); the *hidden idolatry* that thinks "the LORD does not see" against the *grieving remnant* marked to be spared (8-9); and the *glory departing* the defiled temple, yet God a *sanctuary in exile* and the promise of a *heart of flesh* (10-11). Master-findings: **God's severity is the anguish of a betrayed love**; **hidden sin rests on the lie that God is not watching, while grief over sin marks the spared**; and **the hard heart of stone can only be transplanted by God, not repaired by the self.**
- **Threads carried forward:** the new heart / heart of flesh (→ 36:26; ← Jer 31:33); God's presence in exile (→ 43, the returning glory); wounded love beneath judgment (6:9; → 18:23, 33:11); grief over sin (9:4).

---

## Eze 12 - inner-being reading

# Ezekiel 12–13 — inner-being scene reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per unit (provenance `ezekiel-segmentation-batch3-v1-20260704`). Cross-chapter (12:1–13:23), filed at anchor. Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## EZE-see-not-hear-not · Ezekiel 12:1–13:23 · [D, multi] — eyes that see not; false prophets of their own spirit; peace where there is no peace

**The reading.** Ezekiel is told he dwells among "**a rebellious house, who have eyes to see, but see not, who have ears to hear, but hear not**" (12:2). He enacts an exile's departure as a sign. Then judgment falls on the false prophets, "**who prophesy from their own hearts… who follow their own spirit, and have seen nothing!**" (13:2–3); they "**smear [a flimsy wall] with whitewash**" (13:10) and cry "**'Peace,' when there is no peace**" (13:10,16); worst, they "**disheartened the righteous falsely… and encouraged the wicked, that he should not turn from his evil way to save his life**" (13:22). The finding is **faculties *functional yet blind* ("eyes to see, but see not"), false prophets speaking *from their own spirit* ("have seen nothing"), and the double harm of *disheartening the righteous* and *encouraging the wicked*** *(stated)*. The operation is **the interior whose organs of perception *work but do not perceive* (as Isa 6:9, Jer 5:21) — seeing and hearing without receiving; and the *self-sourced* counterfeit word — prophets projecting "their own spirit" and "own hearts" as God's, papering over a doomed wall with "whitewash" and false "peace"; and the moral *inversion* they produce — saddening the faithful and emboldening the wicked, the exact reverse of true prophecy** *(inferred: 12:2's "**eyes to see but see not**" names the recurring inner-being blindness — perception without reception (the same as Eze 42... Isa 6:9); the finding is that the rebellious heart is not short of information but of the *will to perceive*; and 13:2–3's false prophets "**follow their own spirit and have seen nothing**" locate the counterfeit precisely — projecting one's *own* mind as God's word (the same as Jer 23:16); the "**whitewash**" (13:10) is the inner-being image — a *cosmetic covering* over a structurally-doomed wall, the false comfort that hides the real danger; and 13:22 names the *double harm* of the false word — it "**disheartens the righteous**" (grieving those God has not grieved) and "**encourages the wicked**" (confirming them in evil so they "not turn"): the finding is that false comfort is not neutral but *actively harmful in both directions* — it saddens the faithful (making them doubt their true standing) and hardens the sinner (removing the fear that would turn him); the counterfeit word gets the moral polarity exactly backward)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *faculties functional yet blind ("eyes to see but see not, ears to hear but hear not" — perception without reception, the un-willing heart)* (thread — a gem: the rebellious heart short not of information but of the will to perceive, w/ 12:2, Isa 6:9, Jer 5:21, Mark 8:18); *the self-sourced counterfeit word ("follow their own spirit and have seen nothing… from their own hearts")* (thread — a gem: projecting one's own mind as God's word, w/ 13:2-3, Jer 23:16); *whitewash over a doomed wall (cosmetic false comfort hiding the real danger)* (new — a gem: the reassurance that covers rather than cures, w/ 13:10-15, Matt 23:27); *the double harm of the false word ("disheartened the righteous… encouraged the wicked" — false comfort saddening the faithful and hardening the sinner)* (new — a gem: the counterfeit word getting the moral polarity backward, w/ 13:22, Isa 5:20, Jer 23:17).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** faculties functional yet blind; the self-sourced counterfeit word; whitewash over a doomed wall; the double harm of the false word. Chapters 12–13 set the rebellious heart that "sees but does not perceive" beside the false prophets of their own spirit, whose whitewashed "peace" saddens the righteous and hardens the wicked.
- **Threads:** perception without reception (← Isa 6:9, Jer 5:21); self-sourced false word (← Jer 23:16; → 14); double harm of the lie (w/ Isa 5:20, Jer 23:17).

---

## Eze 14 - inner-being reading

# Ezekiel 14–15 — inner-being scene reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per unit (provenance `ezekiel-segmentation-batch3-v1-20260704`). Cross-chapter (14:1–15:8), filed at anchor. Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## EZE-idols-in-the-heart · Ezekiel 14:1–15:8 · [D, multi] — idols set up in the heart; each saves only himself by his own righteousness

**The reading.** Elders come to "inquire" of God, but he exposes their hidden state: "**These men have taken their idols into their hearts, and set the stumbling block of their iniquity before their faces**" (14:3); "**Any one… who takes his idols into his heart… and yet comes to the prophet**" will be answered by God himself, "**that I may lay hold of the hearts of the house of Israel, who are all estranged from me through their idols**" (14:4–5). The summons: "**Repent and turn away from your idols**" (14:6). Then, on a land under judgment, "**even if these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they would deliver but their own lives by their righteousness**" (14:14). The finding is **idolatry located *in the heart itself* ("idols into their hearts", before any outward image) — and the *non-transferability* of righteousness (even the most righteous "deliver but their own lives")** *(stated)*. The operation is **the disclosure that the *real* idol is *inward* — "taken into the heart", set up "before the face" as the thing one actually looks to — so that a person can *outwardly inquire of God* while *inwardly enthroning an idol*; and the sober principle that *righteousness is personal and non-transferable* — no one's virtue, however great, can *cover* another's guilt** *(inferred: 14:3's "**idols INTO THEIR HEARTS**" is the inner-being key — the finding is that idolatry is fundamentally a matter of the *interior*: the idol is not primarily the statue but the thing *enthroned in the heart* and "set before the face" (the object one's inner gaze actually fixes on); a person can come to worship God *outwardly* while an idol occupies the heart *inwardly* — the divided worship God sees straight through ("all estranged from me through their idols", 14:5); the finding is that the decisive question is not what one professes but what one's heart is *set on*; and the cure is inward — "**repent and turn away from your idols**" (14:6), a turning of the heart's fixation; the second finding (14:14) is the *non-transferability of righteousness* — even "Noah, Daniel, and Job" (three bywords of righteousness) could "deliver but their own lives": the finding is that no one's goodness is a *credit* transferable to another — each soul stands or falls on its own relation to God (setting up ch.18's individual responsibility); righteousness is *personal*, not a communal asset one can lean on)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *idols enthroned in the heart ("taken their idols into their hearts… before their faces" — idolatry primarily inward, the thing the heart is set on)* (thread — a gem: the real idol is inward; one can worship God outwardly while an idol occupies the heart, w/ 14:3-5, Col 3:5, Matt 6:24, 1 John 5:21); *the heart's fixation as the decisive question ("all estranged from me through their idols" — not what one professes but what the heart is set on)* (new — a gem: divided worship God sees through, w/ 14:5, Matt 15:8); *turning the heart's fixation ("repent and turn away from your idols" — the inward cure)* (thread — w/ 14:6); *the non-transferability of righteousness ("Noah, Daniel, and Job… would deliver but their own lives" — no one's goodness credited to another; each soul stands on its own)* (new — a gem: righteousness personal, not a communal asset to lean on, w/ 14:14,20, Eze 18:20, Ps 49:7).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** idols enthroned in the heart; the heart's fixation as the decisive question; turning the heart's fixation; the non-transferability of righteousness. Chapters 14–15 locate idolatry *in the heart* (a thing one can hide while inquiring of God) and establish that righteousness is *personal* — even the most righteous save only themselves.
- **Threads:** idols in the heart (← 8:12; w/ Col 3:5, Matt 6:24); non-transferable righteousness (→ 18:20; w/ Ps 49:7).

---

## Eze 16 - inner-being reading

# Ezekiel 16 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per unit (provenance `ezekiel-segmentation-batch3-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## EZE-faithless-bride · Ezekiel 16:1–63 · [D, multi] — the foundling love; trust in one's beauty/gifts; the never-satisfied whoring; the shame that mercy produces

**The reading.** The chapter tells Jerusalem's story as a *rescued foundling*. An unwanted newborn is cast out "**wallowing in your blood**", and God passes by: "**I said to you in your blood, 'Live!'**" (v.6); he raises her, and when she is grown, "**I spread the corner of my garment over you… I made my vow to you and entered into a covenant with you**" (v.8), adorning her until "**your renown went forth among the nations because of your beauty, for it was perfect through the splendour that I had bestowed on you**" (v.14). But then: "**you trusted in your beauty and played the whore… you were not satisfied**" (vv.15,28), even using "**my gold… which I had given you**" to make idols (v.17). Her sister Sodom's guilt is named: "**pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy**" (v.49). And "**How sick is your heart**" (v.30). Yet the ending turns: "**I will remember my covenant with you… I will establish… an everlasting covenant… that you may remember and be ashamed… when I atone for you for all that you have done**" (vv.60,63). The finding is **the *foundling love* that gave the self its very life and beauty, *betrayed* by a heart that "**trusted in its beauty**" and was "**never satisfied**" — and a mercy that *restores* while producing *shame* ("that you may remember and be ashamed… when I atone")** *(stated)*. The operation is **the anatomy of ingratitude and its cure: the self owes God *everything* (life, growth, adornment, renown — all "bestowed"), yet *turns the very gifts against the Giver* — "trusted in your beauty" (making the gift its own glory), used "my gold" for idols (spending God's gifts on rivals to him); the disorder is *insatiable* ("not satisfied" though it multiplied its lovers); and the redemption comes not through the bride's merit but through God *remembering his covenant* and *atoning* — a grace that produces not pride but *shame*, a humbled, silenced gratitude** *(inferred: three inner-being findings. First, the *foundling love* (vv.6–14) — the self's very *existence and worth* are pure gift: it was a dying, unwanted infant to whom God said "**Live!**", and everything it later boasts (beauty, renown) was "**bestowed**" by him; the finding is that the interior owns *nothing* of itself that it did not receive, so all self-glory is stolen glory. Second, the betrayal is *turning the gift against the Giver* — "**you TRUSTED IN YOUR BEAUTY**" (v.15, making God's gift the object of self-confidence) and used "**my gold**" for idols (v.17): the finding is the precise mechanism of ingratitude — the gifts meant to point *to* the Giver become the self's *own glory* and are spent on his rivals; and the appetite is *insatiable* — "**not satisfied**" (vv.28–29) however much it whores (the bottomless quality of misdirected desire); Sodom's guilt (v.49) names the same in social form — "pride, ease, and no aid to the poor", the comfortable self curved in on itself. Third, the *shame that mercy produces* (v.63) — God's atonement does not leave the bride proud but "**ashamed… never to open your mouth again**": the finding is that *being forgiven* rightly produces not entitlement but a *humbled, silenced shame* — the memory of what one was and did, met by grace, closes the boasting mouth; grace received truly *humbles*, it does not inflate)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the foundling love — the self's very life and worth pure gift ("I said to you… Live!"… "perfect through the splendour I had bestowed" — the interior owning nothing it did not receive)* (thread — a gem: all self-glory is stolen glory, w/ 16:6-14, 1 Cor 4:7, Deut 8:17, Hos 2:8); *trusting the gift instead of the Giver ("you trusted in your beauty… made idols of my gold" — the gifts turned into self-glory and spent on God's rivals)* (thread — a gem: the mechanism of ingratitude, the gift meant to point to the Giver becoming the self's boast, w/ 16:15,17, Rom 1:21-23); *insatiable misdirected desire ("you were not satisfied" — the bottomless appetite of the straying heart)* (thread — a gem: misdirected desire never filled, w/ 16:28-29, Eccl 5:10, Jer 2:13); *Sodom's guilt — comfortable self-absorption ("pride, excess of food, prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor")* (new — a gem: the guilt of ease curved inward, w/ 16:49, Amos 6:1-6, Luke 16:19-21); *the shame that mercy produces ("that you may remember and be ashamed… when I atone for you" — grace humbling, not inflating, closing the boasting mouth)* (new — a gem: being forgiven produces humbled silence, not entitlement, w/ 16:60-63, Rom 3:19, Luke 7:47).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the foundling love; trusting the gift instead of the Giver; insatiable misdirected desire; Sodom's guilt of comfortable self-absorption; the shame that mercy produces. Chapter 16 tells the interior's story as a rescued foundling who trusted her God-given beauty, whored insatiably, and is restored by an atoning grace that leaves her humbled and ashamed, not proud.
- **Threads:** all is gift / stolen glory (← Hos 2:8; w/ 1 Cor 4:7); the gift turned against the Giver (← Jer 2:13; w/ Rom 1:21); insatiable desire (← Eccl); Sodom's ease (w/ Amos 6); shame from grace (→ 36:31-32; w/ Rom 3:19).

---

## Eze 17 - inner-being reading

# Ezekiel 17 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per unit (provenance `ezekiel-segmentation-batch3-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## EZE-despised-oath · Ezekiel 17:1–24 · [D, multi] — the sanctity of a sworn oath; faithlessness to a covenant

**The reading.** A riddle of two eagles and a vine tells how Zedekiah, "**one of the royal offspring**", was "**made a covenant with… putting him under oath**" (v.13), "**that the kingdom might be humble and not lift itself up, and keep his covenant that it might stand**" (v.14). But he "**rebelled… by sending his ambassadors to Egypt**" (v.15). God's verdict fixes on the *broken oath*: "**he despised the oath in breaking the covenant… As I live… surely it is my oath that he despised, and my covenant that he broke. I will return it upon his head**" (vv.18–19). The finding is **a *sworn oath treated as binding — and as God's own* — so that faithlessness to one's word ("he despised the oath") is a *sin against God*** *(stated)*. The operation is **the disclosure that a *sworn commitment* has a *sacred weight* — even Zedekiah's oath to a *pagan king* is called by God "**my oath… my covenant**", so that breaking one's word is not merely a political failure but a *betrayal of God*, who stands behind every solemn promise** *(inferred: the striking thing is that Zedekiah's oath was sworn to *Nebuchadnezzar*, a foreign, pagan king — yet God says "**it is MY OATH that he despised, and MY COVENANT that he broke**" (v.19): the finding is that God takes a *sworn word* — even one given to an unbeliever — as *invested with his own name*, so that *keeping faith* is a sacred obligation and *breaking it* is a sin against God himself; the inner-being weight is on the *integrity of one's word* — a promise made "under oath" binds the interior before God, and to "despise" it (treat it lightly, break it for advantage) is to despise the God who witnesses it; the finding is that faithfulness to commitments is not a mere social nicety but a matter of *covenant integrity* that God guards jealously — the trustworthy word is an image of God's own faithfulness, and the broken word a betrayal that "returns upon the head" of the breaker; and the reason the oath bound Zedekiah was "**that the kingdom might be HUMBLE and not lift itself up**" (v.14) — the oath was meant to teach *humility* (accepting one's subordinate place), and its breaking was an act of proud self-assertion seeking Egypt's help rather than accepting the humbling)*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *the sacred weight of a sworn word ("he despised the oath… it is my oath that he despised" — a promise, even to a pagan, invested with God's own name)* (thread — a gem: keeping faith a sacred obligation, breaking one's word a sin against God who witnesses it, w/ 17:18-19, Ps 15:4, Eccl 5:4-5, Matt 5:33-37); *integrity of the word as covenant faithfulness (the trustworthy word an image of God's own faithfulness; the broken word a betrayal that recoils)* (new — a gem: faithfulness to commitments a matter of covenant integrity God guards, w/ 17:19, Num 30:2, Jas 5:12); *the oath meant to teach humility ("that the kingdom might be humble and not lift itself up" — the broken oath an act of proud self-assertion)* (new — w/ 17:14, refusing the humbling).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** the sacred weight of a sworn word; integrity of the word as covenant faithfulness; the oath meant to teach humility. Chapter 17 makes even an oath sworn to a pagan king "God's oath" — so that faithlessness to one's word is a betrayal of the God who witnesses every promise.
- **Threads:** the sworn word / integrity (w/ Ps 15:4, Matt 5:33-37, Jas 5:12); refusing the humbling (← pride themes; Jer 13:15).

---

## Eze 18 - inner-being reading

# Ezekiel 18 — inner-being oracle reading (Phase-2 meaning synthesis)

- **Source:** Phase-1 lexicals per unit (provenance `ezekiel-segmentation-batch3-v1-20260704`). Cited; grounded; *stated* | *inferred*.

---

## EZE-turn-and-live · Ezekiel 18:1–32 · [D, multi] — individual moral responsibility; God's no-pleasure in death; make a new heart, turn and live

**The reading.** God abolishes a fatalistic proverb ("the fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge", v.2): "**Behold, all souls are mine… the soul who sins shall die**" (v.4). Righteousness and guilt are *personal*: the righteous man "**shall surely live**" (v.9); his violent son "**shall surely die; his blood shall be upon himself**" (v.13); and *that* son's righteous son "**shall not die for his father's iniquity**" (v.17) — "**the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself**" (v.20). Then the door of change swings both ways: the wicked who "**turns away from all his sins… shall surely live; none of his transgressions shall be remembered**" (vv.21–22). And the heart of God: "**Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked… and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?**" (v.23); "**Cast away all the transgressions… and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die?… For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone… so turn, and live**" (vv.31–32). The finding is **each *soul answerable for itself* (guilt and righteousness non-transferable), a *door of change open both ways* (the wicked who turns lives, his sins un-remembered), and God's own heart — "**I have no pleasure in the death of anyone… turn, and live**"** *(stated)*. The operation is **three inner-being movements: (1) the *dignity and burden of individual responsibility* — no one is trapped by inherited fate ("the fathers' sour grapes"); each soul stands before God on its *own* ways; (2) the *reality of change* — the past does not fix the future in either direction: the wicked who turns is *not held to* his old sins ("none remembered"), and the righteous who turns is *not credited* his old good — the *present direction* of the heart is what counts; (3) God's *disposition* — he takes *no pleasure* in the sinner's death but *longs* for him to turn and live, so the whole severe chapter rests on a God who *wants life*, not death** *(inferred: (1) the sour-grapes proverb (v.2) expressed *fatalism* — the sense of being doomed by others' sins, unable to change one's lot; God's "**the soul who sins shall die**… the son shall not suffer for the father** (vv.4,20) restores *moral agency and dignity*: the finding is that no interior is *trapped* by inheritance or fate — each stands answerable for its *own* choices, which is both a *burden* (you cannot blame your fathers) and a *dignity* (you are not doomed by them). (2) vv.21–24 establish the *openness of the future* in both directions — the wicked who turns *lives* and his sins are "**not remembered**" (a stunning erasure — the past does not chain him), while the righteous who turns to evil dies (his past good not a permanent credit): the finding is that God reckons by the *present set of the heart*, not the accumulated record — so no one is beyond hope (the past is not destiny) and no one is beyond falling (past goodness is not tenure); what matters is *which way one is now turning*. (3) the theological ground is God's *heart* — "**have I any PLEASURE in the death of the wicked?**" (v.23), "**I have NO PLEASURE in the death of anyone; so TURN, and LIVE**" (v.32): the finding is that beneath all the judgment is a God who *does not want* the sinner to die but *pleads* with him to turn and live — the severity is not vindictiveness but the reluctant necessity of a God whose desire is *life*; and "**make yourselves a new heart**" (v.31) — held together with 11:19/36:26 where God *gives* the new heart — shows the paradox of grace and responsibility: the self is *commanded* to make a new heart (real agency) even as the new heart is ultimately God's *gift* (the command creates the reaching that grace answers))*.

**Characteristics surfaced:** *individual moral responsibility ("the soul who sins shall die… the son shall not suffer for the father" — no interior trapped by inherited fate; each answerable on its own ways)* (thread — a gem: moral agency and dignity restored, both burden and freedom, w/ 18:2-4,20, Deut 24:16, Jer 31:29-30, Rom 14:12); *the future open both ways ("the wicked who turns… none of his transgressions shall be remembered" — the past does not chain, past goodness not tenure; the present direction counts)* (new — a gem: God reckons by the heart's present set, not the accumulated record; no one beyond hope, none beyond falling, w/ 18:21-24, Ezek 33:12-16); *God's no-pleasure in death ("have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked… I have no pleasure in the death of anyone; so turn, and live")* (thread — a gem: beneath all judgment a God who wants life, pleading with the sinner to turn, w/ 18:23,32, 33:11, 2 Pet 3:9, 1 Tim 2:4); *the commanded new heart ("make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit" — real agency held with the gift of 11:19/36:26)* (thread — a gem: the paradox of grace and responsibility; the command creates the reaching grace answers, w/ 18:31, 11:19, 36:26, Phil 2:12-13).

---

## Chapter-level notes
- **Surfaced:** individual moral responsibility; the future open both ways; God's no-pleasure in death; the commanded new heart. Chapter 18 is one of Scripture's clearest windows into God's heart toward the sinner — each soul answerable for itself, the past not destiny in either direction, and a God who takes "no pleasure in the death of anyone" pleading "turn, and live".
- **Threads:** individual responsibility (← Jer 31:29-30; → 33:12-20; w/ Rom 14:12); the future open both ways (→ 33:12-16); no pleasure in death (→ 33:11; w/ 2 Pet 3:9); make/give a new heart (← 11:19; → 36:26).

---
